chapters.title: Chapter 5: Putting Sector Rotation Into Practice

lessons.title: Your Sector Rotation Playbook: A Final Checklist

body.text: A playbook is what turns a framework into a habit. Six questions, asked in the same order every time, with position sizes decided before conviction arrives.

children.text: You have covered the business cycle, India's cycle dashboard, the RBI clock, the rotation model, the evidence for and against it on NSE data, and the practical machinery of vehicles, sizing, funds, and mistakes. This final lesson assembles all of it into a playbook you can actually run, a review rhythm, a journal template, and an honest account of when not to bother.
The Playbook: Six Questions in Order

body.caption: Run these in sequence, every time

cells: Where is India in the business cycle, and which way is momentum moving?
The scorecard: manufacturing and services PMI, GDP growth, non-food credit growth, capacity utilisation, scored on level and direction
Is the RBI and the bond market pushing with the cycle or against it?
The policy dial: stance and repo rate, the yield curve, CPI inflation, plus the real policy rate
Which sectors should the phase and policy dial favour, and why, mechanically?
The rotation clock plus the four mechanics: operating leverage, rate sensitivity, commodity linkage, demand elasticity
Does a structural theme, government policy, global linkage, the monsoon, or index concentration overrule the textbook here?
Is the market already agreeing, and on which timeframe?
Relative strength versus the Nifty 50 on two timeframes, plus the rotation quadrants
Which vehicle, what size, what exit, and what does it cost after tax?
Vehicle comparison, satellite budget and per-sector cap, written thesis and exit conditions

body.text: The order matters. Most investors start at step 5, notice a sector going up, and work backwards to justify it. Running the steps in sequence means your evidence comes before your conviction, which is the only reliable defence against performance chasing.

stats.label: PMI dividing line
stats.context: Above 50 means more firms improving than deteriorating, month on month

stats.label: Capex trigger zone
stats.context: Capacity utilisation at which fresh private investment tends to get committed

stats.label: Satellite budget
stats.context: Of the portfolio, with a per-sector cap; the core stays diversified

stats.label: Equity capital gains tax
stats.context: Short-term versus long-term above ₹1.25 lakh a year, which is why holding periods matter

children.text: A playbook fails if it is run only when markets are exciting. Three routines, at three frequencies, keep it honest.

body.title: Monthly, about 20 minutes
steps: Around the 20th to 25th: note the HSBC India flash PMI for the current month
First working day: final manufacturing PMI; third working day: services PMI; also company auto sales
First days of the month: GST collections, adjusted for festival timing and rate changes
12th: CPI and core inflation, and what they imply for the RBI
20th and 28th: Index of Core Industries and IIP, to see whether leading signals are showing up in output
Update the scorecard: level and direction scores, phase, and policy dial
Update relative strength for your watchlist sectors on two timeframes

body.title: Quarterly, about an hour
steps: Re-read the written thesis for each satellite position and ask whether it still holds
Check whether any position has drifted outside its rebalancing band
Review quarterly results and earnings revisions for your tilted sectors, not just prices
Update capacity utilisation from the RBI OBICUS survey and bank credit trends
Note whether new fund launches or media enthusiasm suggest your theme is now a late signal
Record what you got right and wrong since the last review, with the reason

body.title: Annually, half a day
steps: Audit total satellite exposure against your budget, counting overlapping sectors as one group
Count the sector weights already inside your core, such as financial services in a Nifty 50 fund
Compare your portfolio return with a simple all-core alternative, honestly
Add up the year's trading costs, exit loads, and realised capital gains tax
Plan the coming year's switches around holding periods to avoid unnecessary short-term tax
Review whether your thresholds still make sense after any change to data series or base years
Decide, deliberately, whether to continue running tilts at all

children.text: Here is the playbook applied to the evidence assembled across this course, as of mid September 2026. It is an illustration of the process, not a recommendation, and every reading below will have changed by the time you read this.

cells: Scorecard level +4, momentum +3: expansion. GDP grew 7.8% in April to June 2026, credit growth 19.1%, capacity utilisation 75.6%, but manufacturing PMI has cooled to a five-year low
Repo rate held at 5.25% with a neutral stance, CPI at 4.82% and rising, 10-year yield about 7.01% and higher over the year, crude above US$100
Policy dial neutral, drifting towards headwind
Late cycle with rising inflation favours commodity and energy-linked sectors and defensives with pricing power; rate sensitives and input-cost-heavy consumer sectors are at risk
Prefer commodity, energy, and selected defensives

Structural financialisation supports capital market businesses; government capex supports defence; foreign outflows of about ₹2.37 lakh crore hit large caps; a monsoon 14% below normal hurts rural demand
Overrides matter more than the textbook phase here
Leading on relative strength: defence, pharma, metals, PSU banks, capital markets. Lagging: FMCG, energy, infrastructure. IT shows a short-term bounce inside a 12-month downtrend
Confirmation supports several hypotheses, contradicts energy
Satellites capped at 20% of the portfolio, maximum 10% per sector group, low-cost index funds or liquid ETFs, written thesis and exit conditions for each
Two or three tilts, sized in advance

body.text: Notice step 5 contradicting step 3 on energy: the late-cycle hypothesis favours energy, but relative strength says it has been lagging. That disagreement is information. It means either the market disagrees with your phase call, or the sector has company-specific problems such as the oil marketing squeeze from Lesson 3.3. When steps conflict, size smaller or wait, rather than forcing the trade.

body.title: What a Tilt Can Contribute
body.prompt: Your satellite allocation is 15% of the portfolio, in one sector. Over the next year, that sector beats the Nifty 50 by 12 percentage points. How many percentage points does the tilt add to your portfolio return? Give your answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: 0.15 multiplied by 12 pp gives 1.80 pp. On a ₹20 lakh portfolio, a 15% tilt is ₹3,00,000, and a very good year for it adds about ₹36,000 more than the index would have. That is worth having, and it is also not life-changing. Keeping this arithmetic in mind is the best protection against oversizing a sector call you feel strongly about.

children.text: Applying the Lesson 5.2 template to a ₹20 lakh portfolio at a 20% satellite budget gives ₹4,00,000 for all tilts combined, and a per-sector cap of 10% means no more than ₹2,00,000 in any one sector group. Defence, PSU banks, and other government-linked plays count as one group, not three.
The Journal: One Row Per Decision

The single highest-return habit in this course is writing down each decision when you make it. Without a record, you cannot tell skill from luck, and you will rewrite your reasoning after the fact without noticing.

cells: Expansion maturing, level +4, momentum +3; policy dial neutral, inflation rising
Pharma, via a low-cost sector index fund
Defensive earnings plus dollar revenue in a crude-driven slowdown, with valuations near long-term average
Relative strength leading on both 6-month and 12-month views; 12-month relative return about +27%
Relative strength falls below its 12-month average, or US policy or pricing pressure breaks the earnings thesis, or the position exceeds 10%
31 December 2026, or sooner on an RBI stance change

children.text: When Not to Run This Playbook
You have no emergency fund, or the money is needed within three years. Sector tilts belong to long-horizon money only.
You cannot commit to the monthly and quarterly reviews. A half-monitored rotation strategy is worse than a plain index fund.
You would not hold a tilt through a 40% drawdown lasting two years, which the Nifty Realty and Nifty IT declines of 2024 to 2026 show is entirely normal.
Your core is not yet built. The core comes first; satellites are optional extras.
You find yourself checking prices daily and wanting to act. That is a signal to reduce size, not to refine the model.

body.text: It is a perfectly respectable outcome of this course to decide that you will not rotate at all, and will hold a diversified core instead, while using the cycle framework to understand what you read and to stay calm when a sector you own is having a terrible year. Chapter 4 showed even the textbook clock only partly held in India. Understanding the cycle has value well beyond trading it.

cards.definition: Recovery, expansion, slowdown, contraction, defined by where output sits relative to potential and which way it is heading.
In India the cycle usually shows up as faster or slower growth, not outright contraction; annual GDP has shrunk only once since 1980.
Prices discount future earnings, so leadership changes before the data confirms the phase. The Nifty rallied almost 50% before the record 2020 GDP print.
Score five growth indicators on level and direction, then read the phase off a two-by-two grid; add a policy dial for the RBI, yield curve, and inflation.
Policy affects output after about two quarters and inflation after about three, which is why the RBI acts on forecasts and markets front-run it.
Operating leverage, interest rate sensitivity, commodity linkage, and demand elasticity explain why sectors take turns leading.
Banks and financials, autos, real estate, consumer discretionary: rate sensitive, pent-up demand, high operating leverage.
Capital goods, metals, energy: dependent on capex and commodity prices, and prone to looking cheap on peak earnings.
Structural themes, government capex and policy, global flows and trade, the monsoon, and index concentration can all outrank the textbook phase.
Sector divided by benchmark, rebased to 100. Read two timeframes; a bounce inside a downtrend is not a leadership change.
A diversified core of 70% to 90% plus tilts of 10% to 30% with per-sector caps, so being wrong is survivable.
Trading costs, short-term capital gains tax at 20%, and the behavioural cost of chasing last year's winner, which lagged the Nifty 50 over the last decade.

body.title: Get the Order Right
body.textWithBlank: In the playbook, you assess the cycle phase and the policy dial before forming a sector hypothesis, and you check relative strength ___ forming that hypothesis, so that evidence comes before conviction.
body.explanation: Phase and policy first, hypothesis second, India overrides third, market confirmation fourth, implementation last. Starting with a price chart and working backwards is how performance chasing disguises itself as analysis.

body.title: When the Steps Disagree
body.question: Your phase and policy analysis favours energy, but energy has been lagging the Nifty 50 on both 6-month and 12-month relative strength. What is the most disciplined response?
options: Buy a larger position, because the sector is cheap and your analysis is sound
Treat the disagreement as information: size smaller, wait for confirmation, or investigate what the market knows that your phase call misses
Switch to whichever sector has the highest relative strength
body.explanation: Disagreement between your hypothesis and market confirmation usually means one of two things: the market disagrees with your phase call, or the sector has specific problems your macro view cannot see, such as the oil marketing squeeze of 2022. Neither justifies a larger position. Smaller size, patience, or more investigation are the disciplined responses.

body.title: Write Your Own Playbook
body.scenario: You are setting up your own process from scratch. You have a diversified core, a long horizon, an emergency fund in place, and about 45 minutes a month to spend on this. You want to run at most two sector tilts at a time.
body.prompt: Sketch the playbook you would actually follow: what you check and when, how you size positions, what you write down, and what would make you stop.
body.modelAnswer: A workable version looks like this. Monthly, in about twenty minutes: update the scorecard with the five growth indicators and the policy dial, then update relative strength for a watchlist of six to eight sector indices on 6-month and 12-month views. Quarterly, in about an hour: re-read each tilt's written thesis, check rebalancing bands, look at earnings revisions and capacity utilisation, and note whether media enthusiasm or new fund launches suggest a late signal. Annually: audit total satellite exposure, count the sector weights hidden in the core, total up costs and realised taxes, compare results honestly with an all-core alternative, and decide whether to continue. Sizing: satellites capped at 20% of the portfolio with a maximum of 10% per sector group, only two tilts at a time, each entered only when the phase, the India overrides, and relative strength agree. Journal: one row per decision with date, phase, thesis, evidence, size, exit conditions, and review date. Stop conditions: missing two consecutive quarterly reviews, needing the money within three years, finding myself watching prices daily, or an annual review showing the tilts have added nothing after costs and tax over a full cycle. The framework stays useful even then, because it explains what the economy and the market are doing, whether or not I trade it.

body.text: This lesson, and this course, are educational. Nothing here is investment advice or a recommendation about any sector, stock, index, or fund. All data referenced is as reported at the time of writing and will change, and past patterns do not predict future returns. For decisions about your own portfolio, consider consulting a SEBI registered investment adviser and a qualified tax professional.

The cycle will turn again, and the sectors that lead next will look obvious only afterwards. What you carry forward from this course is not a forecast, but a process: evidence before conviction, sizes before certainty, and a written record either way.

points: Run the playbook in order: phase, policy dial, sector hypothesis, India overrides, relative strength confirmation, then implementation
Build a rhythm, not a reaction: about 20 minutes monthly, an hour quarterly, half a day annually
Remember the anchors: 50 on the PMI, 75% to 80% capacity utilisation for capex, a 10% to 30% satellite budget, and 20% versus 12.5% capital gains tax
Keep the arithmetic in view: a 15% tilt that beats the market by 12 percentage points adds about 1.80 pp to portfolio return
Treat disagreement between your hypothesis and relative strength as information, and respond by sizing smaller or waiting
Journal every decision with thesis, size, exit conditions, and review date, so you can tell skill from luck later
Deciding not to rotate is a legitimate outcome: the cycle framework still helps you understand markets and hold your course through a bad year
